content:
A few days ago, OpenAI accused Apple of improperly submitting new evidence in a trade secrets case. Today Apple fired back, saying OpenAI's response went beyond what court rules permit. Here are the details.

Apple argues that OpenAI's actions are not simply a routine objection to new evidence.

In Apple's lawsuit against two former employees (Chang Liu and Tang Tan), OpenAI, and io Products alleging theft of trade secrets, one of the disputed points involves Apple's request for a temporary restraining order (TRO).

In short, Apple is asking the court to issue a temporary restraining order, arguing that doing so would prevent its trade secrets from being further embedded into OpenAI's hardware development during the course of the case.

In the legal filings submitted by both sides, Apple filed an opposition brief along with five expert declarations. The defendants then accused Apple of improperly introducing new evidence and asked the court to strike portions of the filings.

In its opposition, OpenAI and the other defendants not only claimed that Apple had introduced new evidence, but went further and submitted additional filings to counter Apple's arguments.

Apple responded today to those oppositions, accusing the defendants of doing more than just objecting to new evidence and instead putting forward an entirely new set of arguments and evidence:

Under Local Rule 7-3(d)(1), a party may object to new evidence in an opposition brief, but the rule also states that the filing "shall not include further argument in support of the motion." The defendants did not observe this limit, and instead used their filing to re-litigate the substance of Apple's TRO motion. For instance, the defendants questioned whether Dr. Runge "had any basis to conduct the analyses," whether he had adequately addressed "contradictory evidence," and whether he could establish that certain Apple materials were not publicly available. [⋯] Arguments of this kind are not objections to new evidence. (Stating that "some of the plaintiff's arguments lack evidentiary support or are refuted by other evidence" is not an "objection to evidence.")

Apple also objected to a new declaration submitted by Liu, calling it the defendants' "most egregious overreach":

Notably, when submitting Liu's declaration, the defendants stated that the declaration should only be considered if the court simultaneously decided to admit the Apple evidence that the defendants had challenged.

Apple argues that since the defendants have now put forward an entirely new set of arguments, the court should consider the entire record rather than strike any evidence from Apple's opposition.

The court is scheduled to hear Apple's request for a temporary restraining order on October 14.
